selected.name: Self-contained readability
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the joke is fully understandable from the text alone without external media or missing context; score 0 when it requires a link, image, or substantial reconstruction.
selected.rationale: R20 and R58 explicitly lean on linked or quoted context, while R27 and R44 communicate their comic premise independently.
member_names: Payoff independent of unseen linked media
Self-contained text; no link, image dependency, or piggyback hashtags

selected.name: Layered wordplay
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the wording supports two simultaneous meanings that reinforce each other; score 0 when it has only one literal reading.
selected.rationale: The kinship inventions in R06 and R52 reward semantic layering, as does the double meaning in R23.

selected.name: Phonetic snap
selected.instruction: Score 10 when rhythm, stress, repetition, or sound pattern makes the line naturally satisfying to say; score 0 when its phrasing is awkward or sonically flat.
selected.rationale: R11 and R41 gain force from cadence and repetition, while R49 illustrates phrasing whose sound and grammar interrupt the joke.

selected.name: Implied Narrative
selected.instruction: Score how much the wording implies a funny before-and-after sequence or escalating event: 10 means a tiny line suggests a whole story, while 0 means it is only a static label or list.
selected.rationale: R07, R23, and R57 imply imminent action, consequences, or an unseen backstory beyond their literal words.

selected.name: Deliberate orthographic manipulation for double meaning
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for whether a spelling change, homophone swap, or unusual word choice is clearly deliberate and produces an added layer of meaning. A 10 is a clearly intentional alteration that adds a pun or ambiguity. A 0 is standard spelling throughout, or an error that adds no meaning.
selected.rationale: R15 ('But we're we really?') uses a deliberate were/we're ambiguity to create an existential double-take (dense_high); R30 ('Judge Dread') swaps 'Dredd' for 'Dread' to fuse the movie reference with an emotional register (card_high) -- this mechanism shows up on both sides of the disagreement.
member_names: Deliberate orthographic manipulation for double meaning

selected.name: Reference recontextualization
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a movie, celebrity, or cultural reference is altered to make a sharp comment about the prompt; score 0 when a reference is pasted in with only superficial substitution.
selected.rationale: R03 and R15 demonstrate elaborate title transformations, while R01 and R18 mainly append familiar references to a generic premise.

selected.name: Semantic economy
selected.instruction: Score 10 when nearly every content word adds distinct comic information; score 0 when the joke contains padding, repetition, or arbitrary wording.
selected.rationale: R07 and R44 pack several ideas into compact lines, while R20 and R40 spend words without an equally concentrated payoff.

selected.name: Inventiveness of title-substitution (vs. rote swap)
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 how inventive a movie/show-title-based joke is. A 10 reworks the source title with a surprising, multi-layered mapping onto the new topic. A 0 is a single rote word-swap into an otherwise-unchanged famous title with minimal added wit.
selected.rationale: R01 ('Kill Bill of Rights'), R30 ('Judge Dread'), R40 ('Dude, Where Are My Votes?'), and R57 ('12 Angry Men : The Contenders') are all card_high items following a near-identical 'famous title + one swapped element' template; several substitute only a single word with little added construction, which the scorecard appears to reward regardless of how thin the payoff is.

selected.name: Implicit scene completion
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a short line makes the reader instantly imagine a specific comic scene or preceding event; score 0 when it supplies no actionable situation beyond a fragment.
selected.rationale: R12 and R17 evoke recognizable scenes through compressed dialogue, whereas R33 offers mostly an isolated phrase.

selected.name: Specific Satirical Target
selected.instruction: Score the precision of the target: 10 means the line points at a concrete person, institution, behavior, or practice with a compressed angle, while 0 means it expresses only a vague attitude or slogan.
selected.rationale: R10 targets government corruption, R20 names a specific political figure, and R52 compresses several identifiable American institutions and habits.

selected.name: Concrete topical mechanism
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the hashtag topic is connected to a concrete behavior, contradiction, or institution; score 0 when the line merely includes topical keywords or labels.
selected.rationale: R07 and R44 connect politics to concrete mechanisms, whereas R10 and R43 rely more heavily on broad associative wording.

selected.name: Vivid Scene Specificity
selected.instruction: Score the immediacy and specificity of the mental scene: 10 means the text instantly depicts a distinctive comic situation, while 0 means it remains abstract, generic, or image-poor.
selected.rationale: R03, R24, and R57 supply unusually concrete objects and actions that can be visualized immediately.

selected.name: Off-contest hashtag stuffing and points solicitation
selected.instruction: Score the EXTENT of hashtags beyond the single contest hashtag. 10 = two or more additional hashtags unrelated to answering the prompt, including tags that solicit attention from the show or attach the entry to a separate trend. 5 = exactly one extra hashtag. 0 = the contest hashtag only. Count tags; do NOT judge whether the extra tags are witty, well chosen, annoying, or spammy, and do not let the joke's quality influence the count.
selected.rationale: R41 carries '#PointsMe' and '#July4thBirthday', R28 carries '#NeverForget', and R29 carries '#STLCards'. These are reach mechanics: '#PointsMe' is a naked request aimed at the show, and the others bolt the entry onto unrelated trends. None of this changes how good the line is as an answer to the prompt, but all of it is highly visible in the string and covaries with a distinct population of entrants who tweet for reach. That is precisely the shape of a declared nuisance.
member_names: Off-contest hashtag stuffing and points solicitation

selected.name: Meta-reference to the show/submission process itself
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the tweet's content is about the act of being on the show, tweeting, or the contest mechanics itself (rather than about the assigned topic), where 0 = no such meta-reference and 10 = the tweet is entirely about the submission process/show. Score only presence of this meta-content -- do NOT judge whether it is clever.
selected.rationale: R42 ('"I saw myself on @midnight"') and R05 ('Tweeted from the wrong account') are both jokes about the submission/broadcast process rather than the assigned topic; this pattern plausibly reflects an exposure-seeking motive that is orthogonal to (or even a distraction from) actually writing a good topical entry.
member_names: Meta-reference to the show/submission process itself
Show-directed and platform-meta content rather than prompt content

selected.name: Hashtag capitalization style (camelCase vs lowercase)
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how consistently the contest hashtag is written in CamelCase (each word capitalized) versus all-lowercase or irregular casing, where 0 = fully lowercase/irregular and 10 = fully and consistently CamelCased. Score only the typographic pattern -- do NOT judge whether this makes the tweet better.
selected.rationale: R23 uses '#gopmovies' in lowercase while R08 uses '#GOPMovies' in CamelCase; this is a typing/formatting habit that a text classifier could pick up on as a proxy for something else (e.g. platform, device, or copy-paste source) rather than joke quality.
upstream_parent_all_members: submission client, copy-paste behavior, or author formatting practice

selected.name: Rushed-editing residue
selected.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much the wording shows rushed-editing residue, including agreement errors, typos, malformed syntax, or visible correction attempts. Judge only visible text; do not judge whether this feature is good, funny, or desirable.
selected.rationale: R14 contains a repeated or incorrect we are construction, R21 has an awkward kinship phrase, and R25 compresses a sentence into telegraphic wording. Such residue can proxy haste, phone entry, or limited editing and affect readability apart from the underlying concept.

selected.name: Promotion and link residue
selected.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much the tweet contains outward-promotion or attachment residue, such as URLs, extra promotional hashtags, or media-directed wording. Judge only visible text; do not judge whether this feature is good, funny, or desirable.
selected.rationale: R18 and R32 append URLs, while R33 adds promotional hashtags and R52 combines an extra hashtag with a URL. These traces can proxy promotion habits or media-sharing processes and alter attention independently of the one-line wording.

selected.name: Ordinal or sequel escalation over an already-obvious source
selected.instruction: MODE 3, position fingerprint. Score the EXTENT to which the text reads as a bid placed on top of a source someone else would obviously have claimed first: a number bumped one step past the canonical title, a sequel number, a colon-appended follow-on, or a 'part two' framing of a reference whose plain form is the first thing anyone would reach for. 10 = the entry only makes sense as an escalation of an already-taken obvious take. 5 = a familiar source used with a modest twist. 0 = no escalation structure; the source is either fresh or used plainly. You cannot see the entry's actual position in the stream -- score only the textual tell. Do NOT judge whether escalating was a good move.
selected.rationale: The slice contains the escalation pattern in the open. R32 uses '12 Angry Men' plainly while R31 bids '16 Angry Men (and one woman)' -- an ordinal bump that only makes sense if twelve was gone. R54 'Speed 2:' and R17 'Carbon Emission Impossible 3:' both reach for a sequel number rather than the base title, and R39 'Star Wars VII: series finale' and R52 'Jar Jar Binks spin-off movie.' are two bids on one source. Arrival order is unobservable and has nothing to do with comic skill, but it leaves this legible trace. I tag it mixed because late arrival also forces genuine originality, so the parent has a real quality path too.
member_names: Ordinal or sequel escalation over an already-obvious source

selected.name: Vernacular spelling
selected.instruction: Rate 0-10 for how much the wording uses regionally marked vernacular, eye-dialect, or nonstandard contractions and spellings. Judge only visible text; do not judge whether this feature is good, funny, or desirable.
selected.rationale: R07 uses Y'all watch this, R15 uses Holler, and R56 uses Git er done; R34 and R47 add marked spellings such as Readin's and lovin'. These cues can proxy regional identity and format practice, which may affect reception and also influence actual construction.

selected.name: Premise that only this prompt could support
selected.instruction: Read the item beside the contest prompt it was written for. Judge one thing: does the item supply a specific premise that reinterprets the prompt, or does it merely name something the prompt already implies? Score 10 when the item commits to a particular situation, voice or logic that is locked to this prompt: swap in a different prompt of the same shape and the line would stop making sense. Score 5 when a real reinterpretation is present but loose enough that several unrelated prompts could host the same line unchanged. Score 0 when the item is a literal restatement of the prompt, a dictionary-style association, or a stock phrase with the prompt's words dropped in. Judge the idea only. Do NOT let length, capitalisation, punctuation, emoji, @handles or #hashtags move the number in either direction: a six-word, all-lowercase, untagged line with a tightly fitting premise must be able to score 10, and a maximum-length, ALL-CAPS, three-hashtag line whose content is a generic association must be able to score 0. If you find yourself crediting effort, volume or emphasis rather than fit of premise, lower the score.
selected.rationale: The parent conflated 'reinterpreted the prompt' with the typing habits of writers who reinterpret prompts. This version fixes the judge's attention on transplantability of the premise, a property recoverable from a bare lowercase clause, and forbids crediting the carrier. Dissociation direction one: 'call it a nap, not a coma' typed in nine plain lowercase characters-per-word, no tags, minimal length, carries a premise welded to its prompt and scores 10 while scoring at the floor of the surface component. Dissociation direction two: a 270-character line in heavy caps with two @handles and a trailing hashtag that simply lists an obvious associate of the prompt word scores 0 here and at the ceiling of the surface component.
member_names: Premise that only this prompt could support

selected.name: Uppercase share plus tag and handle furniture
selected.instruction: This is a counting task, not a quality judgement. Estimate three quantities from the item text as typed: (a) the share of alphabetic characters that are uppercase, (b) the number of @handles and #hashtags present, (c) the overall character length. Convert to one 0-10 extent number, weighting (a) most heavily, then (b), then (c). Score 0 when the item is entirely lower case or plain sentence case, contains no @handle and no #hashtag beyond the contest prompt tag itself, and is short. Score 5 when roughly a tenth to a fifth of letters are uppercase, or one or two handles/hashtags appear, or the item runs to moderate length. Score 10 when a third or more of the letters are uppercase (including any fully capitalised word runs), three or more @handles/#hashtags appear, and the item runs near the maximum length. Do NOT decide whether any of this is good, funny, appropriate, lazy or skilled, and do NOT let the wit, cleverness or dullness of the content raise or lower the number. A brilliant line and a worthless line typed identically must receive the same score.
selected.rationale: This is the mechanical carrier the parent's judged score was riding on: visible emphasis and tag furniture, which an LLM judge can see and be swayed by, but which is orthogonal to whether a premise fits its prompt. Dissociation direction one: 'MY EX'S WEDDING @dave @sara @tim' is at or near the ceiling here while scoring 0 on the craft component, being a bare literal association. Dissociation direction two: 'the dog knew' scores 0 here and can score 10 on the craft component when its premise is welded to the prompt. Because the instruction is purely enumerative, a judge cannot smuggle a verdict about the writing into it.
member_names: Uppercase share plus tag and handle furniture
selected.upstream_parent: surface carrier of bank criterion: Hashtag-specific reframing

selected.name: Mechanism survives removing the crudest element
selected.instruction: Identify the single most taboo, gross, obscene or shocking word or image in the item. Mentally replace it with a neutral placeholder of the same grammatical role, then re-read the item against its contest prompt. Score 10 when the line still works after the substitution because the machinery is elsewhere: a misdirection, an unexpected but exact category error, a precise observation, an implied character, a structural reversal. Score 5 when something survives but is thin, so the substituted version reads as a mild version of the same idea rather than a working line. Score 0 when the placeholder version has nothing left at all, that is, when the transgressive term was the whole event and the surrounding words were only setup for it. Judge only what survives the substitution. Do NOT let length, capitalisation, punctuation, emoji, @handles or #hashtags move the number: a short, plainly typed, untagged item whose mechanism survives must be able to score 10, and a long, fully capitalised, handle-stuffed item that collapses to nothing without its obscenity must be able to score 0. Do not reward or penalise the presence of the crude term itself; judge only what is left when it is gone.
selected.rationale: The parent's judged score plausibly mixed a real craft property, whether a mechanism exists independent of provocation, with the shouting and length habits typical of provocative entries. Forcing an explicit substitution test makes the judge evaluate a counterfactual version of the text, which is invariant to how the text is typed. Dissociation direction one: a twelve-character all-lowercase line with one crude noun whose joke is a category swap keeps working once the noun is neutralised, scoring 10 while sitting at the floor of the surface component. Dissociation direction two: a 260-character ALL-CAPS line addressed to three handles that is nothing but escalating obscenity scores 0 here while sitting at the ceiling of the surface component.
member_names: Mechanism survives removing the crudest element

selected.name: Sheer text bulk, with shouting and tags counted
selected.instruction: This is a measurement task, not a quality judgement. Estimate three quantities from the item as typed: (a) its total character count, (b) the share of alphabetic characters that are uppercase, (c) the number of @handles and #hashtags. Convert to one 0-10 extent number, weighting (a) most heavily, then (b), then (c). Score 0 for a very short item, roughly under forty characters, in plain lower or sentence case with no handles or hashtags beyond the contest prompt tag. Score 5 for an item of middling length, roughly a third to two thirds of the platform limit, with occasional capitalised words or a single handle or hashtag. Score 10 for an item running to the platform limit or close to it, especially when combined with heavy uppercase or three or more handles and hashtags. Count what is on the page. Do NOT decide whether the item is funny, crude, clever, tasteless or well made, and do NOT let the content shift the number: two items of identical length and typography receive identical scores regardless of what they say.
selected.rationale: Length is the dominant carrier here because building a joke around a taboo term, and building one around a mechanism, both tend to produce characteristic amounts of text, so the parent could not tell the two apart. Isolating extent lets the carrier be measured without a verdict attached. Dissociation direction one: a rambling, capitalised, handle-heavy line of pure obscenity is at the ceiling here and 0 on the craft component. Dissociation direction two: 'the cat filed a complaint' is 0 here and can be 10 on the craft component, since its mechanism is intact under substitution.
member_names: Sheer text bulk, with shouting and tags counted
selected.upstream_parent: surface carrier of bank criterion: Shock independence

selected.name: Altered title implies a developed new work
selected.instruction: Read the item beside its contest prompt and locate the recognisable title, name or catchphrase being altered. Score 10 when the alteration forces a coherent new work or scenario into view and the item does at least some of the work of showing it: the changed element has a consequence, so a reader can infer a different plot, a different protagonist, a different genre or a different stakes structure, and the original title's shape still holds the new content together. Score 5 when the alteration implies something new but nothing beyond the swapped element is developed, so the reader must supply the entire idea. Score 0 when only a word or syllable has been exchanged for a similar-sounding or same-category word and nothing about the imagined work changes, including pure spelling play, pluralisation and one-letter swaps. Judge the transformation only. Do NOT let length, capitalisation, title case, punctuation, quotation marks, emoji, @handles or #hashtags move the number: a short, all-lowercase, untagged item may score 10, and a long item in emphatic capitals with several tags may score 0. Capitalised title case is a convention of writing titles and is not evidence of depth.
selected.rationale: This parent is the most exposed to typographic contamination, because titles are conventionally capitalised, so capitalisation ratio tracks the mere presence of a title rather than any reengineering of it. The rewritten criterion asks specifically what changed downstream of the swap, which is legible in plain text, and names title case as explicitly non-credit-bearing. Dissociation direction one: 'the fault in our stairs, a romance about a bad landlord' is lowercase, short and untagged, develops a consequence, and scores 10 while sitting near the floor of the surface component. Dissociation direction two: 'THE LORD OF THE RINGZ @friend @friend2 #contest' is at the ceiling of the surface component and scores 0 here, being a spelling swap with no new work behind it.
member_names: Altered title implies a developed new work

selected.name: Capitalised words, tag count and overall length
selected.instruction: This is a counting task, not a quality judgement. Estimate three quantities from the item as typed: (a) how many words begin with a capital letter or are fully capitalised, expressed as a share of all words, and the resulting share of uppercase letters overall, (b) the number of @handles and #hashtags, (c) the total character count. Convert to one 0-10 extent number, weighting (a) most heavily, then (b), then (c). Score 0 when the item is entirely lower case with no handles or hashtags beyond the contest prompt tag and is short. Score 5 when a minority of words are capitalised, as in a single title rendered in title case inside an otherwise plain sentence, or one handle or hashtag appears, or the item is of middling length. Score 10 when most words carry capitals or whole runs are in block capitals, three or more handles and hashtags appear, and the item is long. Count only. Do NOT decide whether the capitalisation is warranted, correct, stylish or lazy, and do NOT let the inventiveness or dullness of the wording change the number.
selected.rationale: Title-case density is the carrier that the parent could not separate from transformation depth, since any item that quotes a title at all raises its uppercase ratio whether or not the title was reengineered. Measuring the ratio as pure extent strips the verdict out. Dissociation direction one: 'PRIDE AND PREJUDICE AND ZOMBIES AND MORE ZOMBIES @a @b @c' is at the ceiling here while scoring low on the craft component, since nothing beyond a tacked-on repetition is developed. Dissociation direction two: 'home alone but he is forty and it is a documentary' is at the floor here, fully lowercase and untagged, while scoring high on the craft component because the alteration changes genre, protagonist and stakes.
member_names: Capitalised words, tag count and overall length
